chapters.title: הָאַרְיֵה הוֹפֵךְ לְמֶלֶךְ הַחַיּוֹת
chapters.orig_title: The Lion Becomes the King of Beasts

s.line: After climbing down from the china wall the travelers found themselves in a disagreeable country,
s.note: מָצְאוּ אֶת עַצְמָם = "found themselves", just as in English. עַצְמוֹ + a possessive ending is the Hebrew "-self": אֶת עַצְמִי (myself), אֶת עַצְמֵנוּ (ourselves). לֹא נָעִים is the everyday "unpleasant"; on its own, לֹא נָעִים also means "how awkward, that's embarrassing".

s.line: full of bogs and marshes and covered with tall, rank grass.
s.note: מְכֻסֶּה (covered) is the pu'al participle; the active pi'el is כִּסָּה (covered something). סָבוּךְ = tangled, a pa'ul participle. In everyday speech it mostly means "complicated": מַצָּב סָבוּךְ (a complicated situation).

s.line: It was difficult to walk without falling into muddy holes, for the grass was so thick that it hid them from sight.
s.note: כָּל כָּךְ … שֶׁ… = "so … that …". לָלֶכֶת and לִפֹּל are infinitives that lose a root letter: הָלַךְ drops the ה and נָפַל drops the נ. מְלֵאֵי is the plural construct of מָלֵא (full).

s.line: However, by carefully picking their way, they got safely along until they reached solid ground.
s.note: עִם זֹאת = "however, even so", a bit more formal than אֲבָל; you will meet it constantly in newspapers. הִתְקַדֵּם (hitpa'el) = to move forward, to make progress: אֵיךְ הַפְּרוֹיֶקְט מִתְקַדֵּם? (how is the project coming along?).

s.line: But here the country seemed wilder than ever,
s.note: יוֹתֵר מִתָּמִיד = "more than ever" (מִן + תָּמִיד, "than always"), a favorite of news writing: הַמְּחִירִים גְּבוֹהִים מִתָּמִיד (prices are higher than ever).

s.line: and after a long and tiresome walk through the underbrush they entered another forest, where the trees were bigger and older than any they had ever seen.
s.note: שֶׁהָעֵצִים בּוֹ ("that the trees in it") is how Hebrew says "where": שֶׁ starts the clause and בּוֹ points back to the forest. גְּדוֹלִים מִ…: an adjective + מִ already means "bigger than", without יוֹתֵר. סְבַךְ (thicket) shares its root with סָבוּךְ above.

s.line: “This forest is perfectly delightful,” declared the Lion, looking around him with joy.
s.note: הִכְרִיז (hif'il) = to declare, announce; הַכְרָזָה = an announcement, as in a public announcement on the news. פָּשׁוּט literally "simple", used as "simply, just" to strengthen an adjective: זֶה פָּשׁוּט מַדְהִים (it's just amazing).

s.line: “Never have I seen a more beautiful place.”
“It seems gloomy,” said the Scarecrow.
s.note: קוֹדֵר = gloomy, dark and depressing. It is used of places, moods and forecasts: תַּמּוּנָה קוֹדֶרֶת (a gloomy picture of the situation).

w: מָה פִּתְאֹם|not at all|~idiom: what suddenly
s.line: “Not a bit of it,” answered the Lion.
s.note: מָה פִּתְאֹם (literally "what, suddenly?") is the everyday spoken "no way, of course not, not at all". You will hear it many times a day in Israel.

w: כָּל הַחַיִּים|all my life|~lit. all the life
s.line: “I should like to live here all my life.
See how soft the dried leaves are under your feet and how rich and green the moss is that clings to these old trees.
s.note: תִּרְאוּ is a future form used as a command ("see!, look!"). Spoken Hebrew uses the future for commands far more often than the true imperative רְאוּ. נִצְמָד לְ… (nif'al) = to cling to, stick close to; the hif'il הִצְמִיד = to press or attach something to.

w: חַיַּת פֶּרֶא|wild beast|~lit. animal of the wild
s.line: Surely no wild beast could wish a pleasanter home.”
s.note: חַיַּת פֶּרֶא = a wild animal (construct of חַיָּה); the plural is חַיּוֹת פֶּרֶא. The adjective פִּרְאִי (wild) comes from the same noun פֶּרֶא. הָיְתָה יְכוֹלָה = "could (if it wanted)", the past of יְכוֹלָה used for "would be able".

w: חַיּוֹת פֶּרֶא|wild beasts|~lit. animals of the wild
s.line: “Perhaps there are wild beasts in the forest now,” said Dorothy.
“I suppose there are,” returned the Lion, “but I do not see any of them about.”
s.note: הֵשִׁיב (hif'il of ש־ו־ב) = replied, a little more literary than עָנָה; the noun תְּשׁוּבָה (answer) has the same root. בַּסְּבִיבָה = "around, in the area": אֲנִי בַּסְּבִיבָה (I'm nearby). אַף אַחַת is feminine because חַיּוֹת is.

s.line: They walked through the forest until it became too dark to go any farther.
s.note: מִדַּי = "too (much)", placed after the adjective: חַם מִדַּי (too hot), יָקָר מִדַּי (too expensive). הִמְשִׁיךְ (hif'il) = to continue; הֶמְשֵׁךְ = continuation, sequel.

s.line: Dorothy and Toto and the Lion lay down to sleep, while the Woodman and the Scarecrow kept watch over them as usual.
s.note: וְאִילּוּ = "while, whereas", used to contrast two people or things: הוּא אוֹהֵב קָפֶה, וְאִילּוּ הִיא שׁוֹתָה תֵּה. שָׁמַר עַל = to guard, look after. כָּרָגִיל = as usual (כְּ + הָ + רָגִיל, "like the usual").

w: יָצְאוּ לַדֶּרֶךְ|set out|~idiom: went out to the road
s.line: When morning came, they started again.
s.note: יָצָא לַדֶּרֶךְ = to set out on a trip. It is also used of projects: הַתָּכְנִית יוֹצֵאת לַדֶּרֶךְ (the program is being launched).

w: חַיּוֹת פֶּרֶא|wild animals|~lit. animals of the wild
s.line: Before they had gone far they heard a low rumble, as of the growling of many wild animals.
s.note: הִתְרַחֵק (hitpa'el, from רָחוֹק far) = to move away, get far off; its opposite is הִתְקָרֵב (to come closer). כְּאִלּוּ = as if; in slang it is also the filler "like".

s.line: Toto whimpered a little, but none of the others was frightened,
and they kept along the well-trodden path until they came to an opening in the wood,
s.note: שְׁבִיל כָּבוּשׁ = a beaten path, pressed down by many feet. כָּבוּשׁ (pa'ul) also means "conquered" and "pickled" (מְלָפְפוֹן כָּבוּשׁ, a pickled cucumber), and כְּבִישׁ (road) has the same root. קָרַחַת = a clearing; a related word is קֵרֵחַ (bald).

s.line: in which were gathered hundreds of beasts of every variety.
s.note: נֶאֶסְפוּ is the nif'al of אָסַף (to collect), here "were gathered, assembled". The noun אֲסֵפָה (a meeting, assembly) is from the same root and comes up in a moment.

s.line: There were tigers and elephants and bears and wolves and foxes and all the others in the natural history,
s.note: שְׁאָר = "the rest", and it stands in construct before the noun: שְׁאָר הַחַיּוֹת, שְׁאָר הַיּוֹם (the rest of the day). הוֹפִיעַ (hif'il) = to appear; הוֹפָעָה = an appearance, and also a show or concert.

s.line: and for a moment Dorothy was afraid.
But the Lion explained that the animals were holding a meeting,
s.note: עָרַךְ = to arrange or hold an event: לַעֲרֹךְ אֲסֵפָה / מְסִבָּה (hold a meeting / throw a party). It also means "to edit": עוֹרֵךְ = an editor. Hebrew keeps the present עוֹרְכוֹת in reported speech, where English shifts to "were holding".

s.line: and he judged by their snarling and growling that they were in great trouble.
s.note: הִסִּיק (hif'il) = to conclude, infer; the set phrase is לְהַסִּיק מַסְקָנוֹת (to draw conclusions). בְּצָרָה = in trouble; צָרָה is a misfortune, a problem.

s.line: As he spoke several of the beasts caught sight of him,
s.note: הִבְחִין בְּ… (hif'il) = to notice, spot; note the preposition בְּ: לֹא הִבְחַנְתִּי בָּךְ (I didn't notice you). The same root gives בְּחִינָה (an exam) and מִבְחָן (a test).

w: כְּאִלּוּ בְּמַטֵּה קֶסֶם|as if by magic|~idiom: as if with a magic wand
s.line: and at once the great assemblage hushed as if by magic.
s.note: הִשְׁתַּתֵּק (to fall silent) is hitpa'el of שָׁתַק (to be silent). When the root starts with שׁ, the ת of the prefix swaps places with it: not *הִתְשַׁתֵּק but הִשְׁתַּתֵּק. כְּאִלּוּ בְּמַטֵּה קֶסֶם = "as if by a magic wand", the usual Hebrew way to say "as if by magic".

s.line: The biggest of the tigers came up to the Lion and bowed, saying:
s.note: הַגָּדוֹל בַּטִּיגְרִיסִים = "the biggest of the tigers": הַ + adjective + בְּ + group is one way to form a superlative. In conversation you would more often hear הַטִּיגְרִיס הֲכִי גָּדוֹל.

w: בָּרוּךְ הַבָּא|welcome|~set phrase: blessed is the one who comes
s.line: “Welcome, O King of Beasts!
s.note: בָּרוּךְ הַבָּא = welcome (to one man); בְּרוּכָה הַבָּאָה to a woman, בְּרוּכִים הַבָּאִים to a group, the words on every welcome sign. The traditional reply is בָּרוּךְ הַנִּמְצָא.

s.line: You have come in good time to fight our enemy and bring peace to all the animals of the forest once more.”
s.note: נִלְחַם בְּ… = to fight (against) someone. It is nif'al in form but active in meaning, and it takes בְּ. מִלְחָמָה (war) shares the root ל־ח־ם. בְּדִיּוּק בַּזְּמַן = just in time.

s.line: “What is your trouble?” asked the Lion quietly.
s.note: מָה מַטְרִיד אוֹתְךָ? = "what's bothering you?", a very common question. אֶתְכֶם is the standard form of "you (pl.)" as an object; in speech many people say אוֹתְכֶם.

s.line: “We are all threatened,” answered the tiger, “by a fierce enemy which has lately come into this forest.
s.note: מְאֻיָּם is a pu'al participle, "threatened"; the pi'el אִיֵּם עַל = threatened (someone), and אִיּוּם = a threat, a word you will see in every news report. עַל יְדֵי = "by" after a passive. לָאַחֲרוֹנָה = lately, recently.

s.line: It is a most tremendous monster, like a great spider,
s.note: מִפְלֶצֶת (monster) is feminine, so the tiger keeps using feminine forms for it: יֵשׁ לָהּ, הִיא תּוֹפֶסֶת. When the narrator calls it עַכָּבִישׁ (masculine), the forms switch to masculine. דּוֹמֶה לְ… = similar to, resembling.

w: יֵשׁ לָהּ|it has|~lit. there is to her
s.line: with a body as big as an elephant and legs as long as a tree trunk.
s.note: גֶּזַע = a tree trunk, and also a race or breed: כֶּלֶב מִגֶּזַע (a purebred dog). רֶגֶל is feminine, so it is רַגְלַיִם אֲרֻכּוֹת.

w: יֵשׁ לָהּ|it has|~lit. there is to her
s.line: It has eight of these long legs,
s.note: שְׁמוֹנֶה is the feminine "eight", used here because רֶגֶל is feminine. With a masculine noun it is שְׁמוֹנָה: שְׁמוֹנָה יָמִים.

s.line: and as the monster crawls through the forest he seizes an animal with a leg and drags it to his mouth,
s.note: זוֹחֵל = crawling; a זוֹחֵל is also a reptile, and a baby who crawls זוֹחֵל too. גָּרַר = to drag; גְּרָר = a tow truck or trailer.

s.line: where he eats it as a spider does a fly.
Not one of us is safe while this fierce creature is alive,
s.note: כָּל עוֹד = "as long as": כָּל עוֹד אֲנִי פֹּה (as long as I'm here). בָּטוּחַ means both "safe" and "sure": אַתָּה בָּטוּחַ? (are you sure?). מֵאִתָּנוּ = "of us"; people prefer it to מִמֶּנּוּ, which can also mean "from him".

s.line: and we had called a meeting to decide how to take care of ourselves when you came among us.”
s.note: כִּנֵּס (pi'el) = to convene, call together. The same root gives כֶּנֶס (a conference), נִכְנַס (to enter) and הַכְּנֶסֶת (Israel's parliament). שָׁמַר עַל עַצְמוֹ = to take care of oneself; תִּשְׁמֹר עַל עַצְמְךָ = take care!

s.line: The Lion thought for a moment.
“Are there any other lions in this forest?” he asked.
s.note: אֲרָיוֹת is the irregular plural of אַרְיֵה: masculine, but ending in וֹת. עוֹד before a noun = "more, other": עוֹד קָפֶה? (more coffee?).

s.line: “No; there were some, but the monster has eaten them all.

w: וְחוּץ מִזֶּה|and besides|~fixed phrase: and apart from this
s.line: And, besides, they were none of them nearly so large and brave as you.”
s.note: חוּץ מִזֶּה = "besides, apart from that", very common when adding a point. אֲפִלּוּ לֹא קָרוֹב = "not even close", exactly as in English.

w: אָשִׂים קֵץ|I put an end|~idiom: put an end (pa'al · שׂ־י־ם)
s.line: “If I put an end to your enemy, will you bow down to me and obey me as King of the Forest?” inquired the Lion.
s.note: שָׂם קֵץ לְ… = to put an end to, a higher-register phrase from the news: לָשִׂים קֵץ לָאַלִּימוּת (to end the violence). צִיֵּת לְ… (pi'el) = to obey; צַיְּתָן = obedient. הַאִם marks a yes/no question in careful speech.

s.line: “We will do that gladly,” returned the tiger;
and all the other beasts roared with a mighty roar: “We will!”
s.note: שָׁאֲגוּ שְׁאָגָה: verb + noun from the same root, as in קָד קִידָה. אַדִּיר = mighty, and in slang "awesome": הָיָה אַדִּיר!. The beasts' answer נַעֲשֶׂה! may remind you of the Torah's נַעֲשֶׂה וְנִשְׁמָע ("we will do and we will obey").

s.line: “Where is this great spider of yours now?” asked the Lion.
“Yonder, among the oak trees,” said the tiger, pointing with his forefoot.
s.note: הִצְבִּיעַ עַל (hif'il) = to point at. The same verb means "to vote": הַצְבָּעָה = a vote, לְהַצְבִּיעַ בַּבְּחִירוֹת = to vote in the elections. קִדְמִי = front (adj.); אֲחוֹרִי = back, rear.

s.line: “Take good care of these friends of mine,” said the Lion, “and I will go at once to fight the monster.”
s.note: הֵיטֵב = well, thoroughly, a more formal word than טוֹב: תַּקְשִׁיבוּ הֵיטֵב (listen carefully). Again a future form, תִּשְׁמְרוּ, is doing the work of a command.

s.line: He bade his comrades good-bye and marched proudly away to do battle with the enemy.
s.note: נִפְרַד מִ… (nif'al) = to say good-bye to, to part from; it also means "to split up": הֵם נִפְרְדוּ (they broke up). פְּרֵדָה = a parting. צָעַד = to march, to step; צַעַד = a step.

s.line: The great spider was lying asleep when the Lion found him,
s.note: יָשֵׁן (sleeping) and יָשָׁן (old, not new: מְכוֹנִית יְשָׁנָה) look identical without vowels: ישן. Context tells you which one it is.

w: עִקֵּם אֶת הָאַף|turned up his nose|~idiom: twisted the nose
s.line: and it looked so ugly that its foe turned up his nose in disgust.
s.note: מְכֹעָר (ugly) is pu'al in form, like מְאֻשָּׁר. עִקֵּם אֶת הָאַף ("twisted the nose") = to turn up one's nose, to show disdain: הוּא עִקֵּם אֶת הָאַף עַל הָאֹכֶל (he turned up his nose at the food).

s.line: Its legs were quite as long as the tiger had said,
and its body covered with coarse black hair.
s.note: גַּס = coarse, rough, and also "rude, vulgar": אַל תִּהְיֶה גַּס (don't be rude). שֵׂעָר (hair) is a collective noun, so the adjectives stay singular.

w: הָיָה לוֹ|it had|~lit. there was to it
s.line: It had a great mouth, with a row of sharp teeth a foot long;
s.note: שִׁנַּיִם is feminine (שֵׁן, a tooth), so the adjective is חַדּוֹת. A foot is about thirty centimeters, so the measure is given in metric, as an Israeli reader would expect.

s.line: but its head was joined to the pudgy body by a neck as slender as a wasp’s waist.
s.note: מְחֻבָּר (pu'al) = joined, connected; the pi'el חִבֵּר = to connect, and also to add up numbers (חִבּוּר = addition). מָתְנַיִם (waist), pronounced motnayim, is a dual form like עֵינַיִם.

s.line: This gave the Lion a hint of the best way to attack the creature,
s.note: הַ… בְּיוֹתֵר is the standard superlative in writing: הַטּוֹבָה בְּיוֹתֵר = the best; in speech, הֲכִי טוֹבָה. תָּקַף = to attack; הַתְקָפָה = an attack, a news word.

s.line: and as he knew it was easier to fight it asleep than awake, he gave a great spring and landed directly upon the monster’s back.
s.note: מֵאֲשֶׁר = "than" before a whole phrase or clause; before a simple noun מִ is enough. נָחַת = to land, used of planes too: הַמָּטוֹס נָחַת, נְחִיתָה = landing. זִנֵּק זִנּוּק is again verb + noun from one root.

s.line: Then, with one blow of his heavy paw, all armed with sharp claws, he knocked the spider’s head from its body.
s.note: חָמוּשׁ (pa'ul) = armed, a word you will often meet in the news. הֵעִיף (hif'il of עָף, to fly) = "made fly, sent flying"; in everyday speech it also means "threw out, fired": הֵעִיפוּ אוֹתוֹ מֵהָעֲבוֹדָה (they fired him).

s.line: Jumping down, he watched it until the long legs stopped wiggling,
s.note: הִפְסִיק (hif'il) + infinitive = to stop doing something: הִפְסַקְתִּי לְעַשֵּׁן (I stopped smoking). הִתְפַּתֵּל = to wriggle, twist; a winding road is כְּבִישׁ מִתְפַּתֵּל.

s.line: when he knew it was quite dead.
The Lion went back to the opening where the beasts of the forest were waiting for him and said proudly:
s.note: חִכָּה לְ… (pi'el) = to wait for: אֲנִי מְחַכֶּה לְךָ (I'm waiting for you). שֶׁשָּׁם ("that there") = where.

s.line: “You need fear your enemy no longer.”
s.note: כְּבָר לֹא = "no longer, not anymore": הוּא כְּבָר לֹא גָּר פֹּה (he doesn't live here anymore). פָּחַד מִ… takes מִ; the infinitive you will hear most is לְפַחֵד.

s.line: Then the beasts bowed down to the Lion as their King,
and he promised to come back and rule over them as soon as Dorothy was safely on her way to Kansas.
s.note: הִבְטִיחַ (hif'il) = to promise; the root ב־ט־ח also gives בָּטוּחַ (safe, sure) and בִּטָּחוֹן (security). בְּרֶגַע שֶׁ… = "as soon as", followed by the future. מָלַךְ עַל = to rule over; מֶלֶךְ has the same root.
